Set posted[platform] to an ISO timestamp as each goes out, then commit. Check every link keeps its own platform's utm_source before posting. Every example in this copy is a real failure in this estate; re-verify the SPF one before posting, because it is the one being fixed on 17 August.
title: A system reporting on itself
_why_this_campaign_exists: Every post about p(Doom)1 so far has been about p(Doom)1. This one is about the working: three failures from the last fortnight, all of which are the same failure. In each case a system was asked whether it had succeeded and said yes, and the answer was believed because it came back green. That is not a lesson anyone needs delivered as a lesson; it is three short stories that land on their own if they are told accurately and then left alone. The reason it is worth publishing is that it is the most credible thing this project can say about itself - not that we are careful, but that we found these, wrote them down with numbers, and changed the checks.

_facts_this_copy_must_not_break.constraint: The rule is: a check must take at least one INPUT FROM OUTSIDE the system it is checking, and must not derive what to look for from that same system. Quote it, do not reword it. In particular NEVER write it as 'output from inside' -- that inverted form was written into pdoom-data's CLAUDE.md on 2026-08-02 and propagated into three repos and two printed sheets before it was caught, and it passes the exact failure the rule exists to catch.
_facts_this_copy_must_not_break.why_not_machine: The canonical wording lives in a GitHub issue body in another repo (pdoom1#1075). Nothing in this repo holds it, and checking our prose against our own restatement of it would be checking a claim against a claim -- which is the defect the rule itself describes.
_facts_this_copy_must_not_break.source: pdoom1#1075, the canonical wording, restored by coordination#5. Quoted in coordination PROTOCOL_UPDATES_2026-08-02.md:57 and 63, coordination LESSON_2026-08-15_look-at-the-thing.md:58, coordination HANDOVER_2026-08-15_pdoom1-mail-transmission.md:134, and pdoom-data CLAUDE.md, which also records the inversion and its blast radius.

That is scheduled to be fixed. If pdoom1-website#321 is closed, the present tense is a lie and the paragraph must be rewritten into the past tense before posting -- and the same-day check is not that the DNS was edited, it is that a probe message arrived in the inbox.

Three things went wrong here in the last fortnight, and it took the third one to notice they were the same thing.

The first is the website's feedback form. It showed every visitor "Report Submitted!" and delivered nothing. The send call returned true, and the success page was generated before delivery was even attempted; a probe on 14 August came back {"ok":true} and had still not arrived thirty-four minutes later. The cause is that the domain has never published an SPF record while its mail is hosted elsewhere, so the receiving side saw its own hosted domain arriving unauthorised from a shared-hosting IP and quietly dropped it. What makes it worth writing down is not the misconfiguration; it is the comment sitting beside the sender address in our own source, which reads "same domain -> passes SPF on DreamHost". A claim about DNS, in a file, never once checked against DNS.

The second is printing. Six jobs were reported as printed and five of them had been cancelled at the device. The check polled the print queue and saw it empty, which it was; a queue empties identically whether a job printed or was killed at the panel. The queue was reporting the printing system's own intake, accurately, and intake is not outcome.

The third is a redaction tool. It strips email addresses out of a public dataset, and it carried a verifier that reported the file clean while ten records were still publishing live addresses. The extraction that produced the text had inserted a space inside each domain; the redactor's pattern required a dot immediately after the domain's first token, so it matched nothing, and the verifier - built on that same pattern - saw nothing to report. What caught it was a separately written scanner giving a different answer.

The obvious fix on that last one is to make detection and verification share a single function, and that is exactly wrong: a defect in the shared function then becomes invisible to both. So the rule we work to now, and I am quoting it rather than rewording it, is that a check must take at least one input from OUTSIDE the system it is checking, and must not derive what to look for from that same system. Two clauses, because each one of these failures passes a single-clause version.

The form has been rerouted to a plain email address until the DNS is fixed and a test message has been seen arriving in an inbox - not merely until the DNS is edited. The printer tool now validates the file with a different program than the one that made it and reads the job's terminal state; it is also honest that it still cannot tell whether there is paper in the tray, because only a person can see that. The redaction scan runs on every push, gated on the independent scanner rather than on the redactor's pattern, and it has been observed going red, which is the only evidence that a green means anything.

copy.devlog:
# A system reporting on itself

This one is not about the game. It is about the working, and about three failures from the last fortnight that turned out to be one failure wearing different clothes.

## The form that always succeeded

The site has a feedback form. It POSTs to a small PHP handler, which calls the platform's mail function, which returns true. The success page - "Report Submitted!" - is generated before delivery is attempted, and the mail function returns true whether or not anything is ever delivered. On 14 August a probe went through it, came back `{"ok":true}`, and had not arrived thirty-four minutes later.

The reason nothing arrives is dull: the domain has never published an SPF record, its MX is Google, and the mail leaves from a DreamHost IP, so Google sees its own hosted domain arriving unauthorised from somewhere it has no reason to trust and does not deliver it. That is a fifteen-minute DNS change, and it is booked for Monday.

The part I keep re-reading is line 23 of the handler. Beside the constant that sets the sender address there is a comment:

> `// same domain -> passes SPF on DreamHost`

A claim about DNS, written into a source file, sitting there for months, and never once checked against DNS. Nobody lied; somebody reasoned about what should follow from the configuration and then wrote the conclusion down in a place where it reads like an observation. `pdoom1-website#321`

The fix in the meantime is to point the navigation at a plain mailto address, which works because the visitor's own mail client sends from their own provider and never touches ours. The revert condition is written into the markup: put the form back once the SPF record is live AND a probe has been confirmed arriving in the inbox. Not once the DNS has been edited. The edit is not the outcome either.

## Six printed, five cancelled

Same week, different subsystem. Six print jobs were reported as printed. Five of them had been cancelled at the device.

The check polled the print queue and found it empty. It was empty. A job cancelled at the panel leaves the queue in exactly the state a printed job leaves it in; the queue is the printing system reporting on its own intake, and intake is not outcome. Six greens, one real print.

The replacement does three things differently. It validates the artefact with a different program than the one that generated it, on the principle that a generator cannot certify its own output. It reads the job's terminal state rather than the queue's emptiness. And it exits non-zero when it fails, which sounds too obvious to state until you notice how many checks in a codebase discard the exit code of the thing they invoke.

It is also candid about where it stops: it still cannot see whether there is paper in the tray. Nothing in the software can. Only a person standing next to the machine can close that loop, and saying so is better than a check that implies otherwise.

## The verifier that agreed with itself

The third one is the oldest and the one I find hardest to look at directly.

A dataset here is built from extracted PDF text, and academic PDF front matter is contact details, so there is a tool that strips email addresses before anything is published. It has a verifier. The verifier reported the file clean. Ten records in the public zone were still carrying live addresses, and a tracked intermediate zone that no redaction run had ever listed held another three hundred and six occurrences.

The cause is one piece of damage doing two jobs. The PDF extraction had inserted a space inside each domain - `uni -tuebingen.de`, `louisville. edu`, `cbs .dk` - and the redactor's pattern requires a dot immediately after the domain's first token, so it matched nothing. The verifier was built on that same pattern. The damage that made the addresses hard to read is the damage that made them invisible to the scanner, and the scanner reported that as cleanliness.

There was an earlier count of four records. It came from reading the file. The count of ten came from running a scanner that had not existed when the first count was made.

The tempting fix is to have detection and verification share one function so they can never disagree. That is the wrong direction: a defect in the shared function is then invisible to both, which is what had already happened. What actually found this was a separately written scanner giving a different answer. The scan now runs in CI, gated on that independent scanner, and it has been observed going red - which is the only thing that makes its green worth anything.

## The rule

Quoted, not reworded, because this one was written down backwards once and the inverted version propagated through three repositories and two printed sheets before anybody noticed:

> A check must take at least one input from **outside** the system it is checking, and must not derive what to look for from that same system.

Two clauses, and each of the three failures above defeats a version with only one. The mail function observed the wrong thing. The queue observed the right object's wrong property. The verifier observed correctly and looked for the wrong thing, because what to look for came out of the system under test.

A sentence I have stopped being able to un-see: nearly every green in an estate this size is a system being asked whether it worked.
